Arthur Miller. The playwright who made American drama grapple with conscience and collective pressure, who wrote plays that moved audiences to tears while asking ruthless questions about ethics and complicity. His work defined how we think about the American dream and its catastrophic failures.

Death of a Salesman arrived in nineteen forty-nine and became the tragedy that explains American ambition to itself. A traveling salesman chasing the dream until he shatters on it—Pulitzer Prize winner, and it remains the play people return to when they need to understand American delusion and decline. But Miller didn't just explore personal failure. The Crucible, written in nineteen fifty-three and set during the Salem witch trials, was really about McCarthyism and mass hysteria—about how ordinary people get swept into collective madness. A View from the Bridge, five years later, gave us an Italian-American longshoreman consumed by jealous passion, written with Shakespearean compression and inevitability.

Miller won the Pulitzer Prize twice, and he became one of the most performed American playwrights of the twentieth century. Beyond the plays, he was a public intellectual: he testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee during the Red Scare and refused to name names, putting his career on the line for principle. His dramas always combine social realism with symbolic depth—characters caught in systems designed to make them complicit, forced to choose between survival and conscience.

So when we think about American drama, about moral conscience and the individual's ethical responsibility, we're thinking in Arthur Miller's categories. His plays are how an entire generation learned to ask what we owe to each other.
